slo.text_verbatim: Evaluate the determinant and inverse of a matrix of order 2 by 2.
slo.success_criterion: By the end you can evaluate |A| for any 2x2 matrix, say whether it is singular or non-singular, and find A^-1 where it exists.

objectives: I can evaluate $|A| = ad - bc$ for a 2x2 matrix.
I can decide if a matrix is singular or non-singular from its determinant.
I can find the adjoint and the inverse of a non-singular 2x2 matrix.

spec.title: THE DETERMINANT AS AN AREA
spec.caption: Columns of $A = \begin{bmatrix}5 & 6\\ 2 & 3\end{bmatrix}$ span this parallelogram; area = $|A| = 3$.

items: Determinant and inverse formulas are fixed: watch one, work one together, try one alone.
Determinant of $A = \begin{bmatrix}a & b\\ c & d\end{bmatrix}$ is $|A| = ad - bc$ — a number, not a matrix.
Adjoint swaps primary-diagonal entries, then flips sign of secondary-diagonal entries.

blocks.text: If $|A| = 0$, pupils may try $A^{-1} = \frac{1}{|A|}\text{adj}\,A$ — ask: what does dividing by zero give? No inverse exists.

blocks.title: Spot the marked error
blocks.prompt: A pupil found $A^{-1}$ for $A=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 4\\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}$. One line is marked wrong. Write it correctly.
steps: adj $A = \begin{bmatrix}2 & -4\\ -1 & 3\end{bmatrix}$  ✗ INCORRECT — this swapped $b$ and $c$ instead of $a$ and $d$
correct: adj $A = \begin{bmatrix}2 & -4\\ -1 & 3\end{bmatrix}$ comes from swapping $a$ with $d$ and negating $b$ and $c$: ____
blocks.answer: adj $A = \begin{bmatrix}2 & -4\\ -1 & 3\end{bmatrix}$, so $A^{-1} = \frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}2 & -4\\ -1 & 3\end{bmatrix}$. The error was swapping the wrong pair.

mistakes.you_ask: Read the formula off the board — is the second term added or subtracted?
Which pair swaps places, and which pair only changes sign?
If $|A| = 0$, does $A^{-1}$ exist at all? What do we call that matrix?

one_screen: Objective: pupils evaluate $|A| = ad - bc$ for a 2x2 matrix, decide if it is singular or non-singular, and find $A^{-1}$ where it exists. Prerequisite check: work out $(5 \times 3) - (6 \times 2)$; answer $15 - 12 = 3$, this is exactly the determinant pattern used all lesson. Worked example, find $A^{-1}$ for $A = \begin{bmatrix}5 & 6\\ 2 & 3\end{bmatrix}$. Step 1: $|A| = 5(3) - 6(2) = 15 - 12 = 3$. Step 2: since $|A| \neq 0$, $A$ is non-singular so an inverse exists. Step 3: form adj $A$ by swapping the primary diagonal and negating the secondary diagonal, giving $\begin{bmatrix}3 & -6\\ -2 & 5\end{bmatrix}$. Step 4: $A^{-1} = \frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}3 & -6\\ -2 & 5\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}1 & -2\\ -\frac{2}{3} & \frac{5}{3}\end{bmatrix}$. Practice one, $F = \begin{bmatrix}3 & 1\\ 2 & 4\end{bmatrix}$, find $|F|$, answer $12 - 2 = 10$. Practice two, is $F$ singular, answer $10 \neq 0$ so non-singular. Practice three, $G = \begin{bmatrix}2 & 6\\ 1 & 3\end{bmatrix}$, does $G^{-1}$ exist, answer $|G| = 0$ so $G$ is singular and has no inverse. Misconception to watch: when $|A| = 0$ some pupils still try $A^{-1} = \frac{1}{|A|}\text{adj}\,A$ anyway, stop them and ask what dividing by zero gives, a singular matrix simply has no inverse. Exit question: for $C = \begin{bmatrix}2 & 4\\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}$, is $C$ singular?
